content: 1. A study conducted in Zambia by Torpey et al. (2010) aimed to reduce pediatric HIV infections by estimating mother-to-child transmission rates within a program setting. However, no data were available on the combined use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and breastfeeding. 2. Van Lettow et al. (2012) evaluated the uptake and outcomes of a prevention-of-mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) program in Zomba District, Malawi. The study assessed all transmission cases while excluding deaths within 24 hours of birth. 3. Alvarez-Uria (2012) conducted research in India across three hospitals in Antapur. The study examined the use of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) during breastfeeding (BF) and replacement feeding (RF) from the first antenatal visit through six months postpartum. Outcomes included transmission and mortality rates from the first week of life. 4. Thistle et al. (2015) studied HAART use in Zimbabwe at the Salvation Army Hospital. 5. Homsy et al. (2010) conducted a study in Uganda (Tororo and Busia Districts) on HAART use during breastfeeding. The study followed mothers from their first antenatal visit through six months postpartum, with outcomes assessed at three, six, and 18 months, including transmission and mortality rates. 6. Peltier et al. (2009) examined HAART use in Rwanda across four government-run health facilities. 7. Marazzi et al. (2009) conducted research in Mozambique on HAART use during breastfeeding. The study followed mothers for 15 weeks postpartum, with outcomes assessed at five and 12 months, including transmission and mortality rates. 8. Kilewo et al. (2009) studied HAART use in Tanzania (Dar es Salaam) during breastfeeding. The research followed mothers for 34 weeks postpartum, with outcomes assessed at six, nine, 12, and 18 months, including transmission and mortality rates. 9. Tonwe-Gold et al. (2007) conducted a study in Côte d’Ivoire at two community-based antenatal clinics in Abidjan. The research examined the use of HAART, single-dose nevirapine (sdNVP), and short-course antiretroviral therapy (scARV) during breastfeeding and replacement feeding. 10. Sagay et al. (2015) studied HAART use in Nigeria, focusing on lifelong ART during breastfeeding. Outcomes were assessed at one year and 18 months, including transmission and mortality rates. 11. Ngoma et al. (2015) conducted research in Zambia on lifelong HAART use during breastfeeding. 12. The Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale was modified for this study. A maximum of one star could be awarded for each item in the selection and outcome categories. The comparability of cohorts was not applied in this study, as all mothers were exposed to ART, and the outcome was HIV-free survival. This outcome was not adjusted for confounders or covariates. 13. Adherence to ART was assessed based on detailed reporting and adherence rates at the end of the study. High adherence rates or non-adherence rates below 20% were considered unlikely to introduce bias. 14. Treatment eligibility was categorized as follows: lifelong ART for all women regardless of HIV disease progression, ART provided for PMTCT for six months or longer if breastfeeding continued, or ART eligibility based on CD4 count or disease progression. 15. 16. The duration of breastfeeding was assessed based on clear reporting of exclusive breastfeeding up to six months, continued breastfeeding for one year, cessation at six months, or insufficient detail. 17. The outcome of interest was HIV-free survival, defined as the absence of infant death or HIV transmission. This was assessed through protocol visits, laboratory procedures, and clinical records. Studies that only reported HIV transmission or death without providing HIV-free survival estimates did not score on this item. 18. Timing of outcome assessment was evaluated based on whether infection or survival was assessed at multiple time points during the trial. Studies that only reported infections between age points without providing a denominator at risk did not score on this item.
